newsitem.title: PERU: Peru leader wins high marks for crisis handling.
newsitem.headline: Peru leader wins high marks for crisis handling.

text.p: In his turbulent six-year rule, President Alberto Fujimori has survived just about everything Peru could throw at him.

An economy in collapse. A ferocious communist revolution. A military coup attempt. A flourishing narcotics trade. A corrupt and incompetent judiciary and Congress. And, for good measure, a wife who turned against him.

Such experiences helped prepare the president for his current showdown with Marxist hostage-takers who staged one of the most audacious assaults in guerrilla history. And 42 days after the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence, where it still holds 72 hostages, Fujimori, 58, is winning widespread, if guarded, praise for his handling of the crisis so far.

"He is certainly no stranger to crisis management," David Scott-Palmer, an author on Peru's guerrilla conflicts, said in a telephone interview from Boston. "Under the circumstances, which are extraordinarily difficult and totally unexpected, he has done as good a job as could possibly be expected."

Analysts highlighted Fujimori's successful combination of a tough and consistent government position with the avoidance of bloodshed. But they warned he was walking a tightrope, where one false move could bring violence.

"The end results will speak for themselves," Sandy Markwick of consulting firm Control Risks Group said from Washington. "But it seems he is handling it pretty well. Above all, he hasn't sent the troops in, and I believe he's right to hold back on that."

Markwick said Fujimori was justified in maintaining a hard line on the rebels' principal demand for the release of jailed comrades and acted wisely in proposing an independent body to oversee peace talks. "But he should consider the question of prison conditions and the broader question of the justice system, which has led to some very questionable convictions."

Fujimori was in a dilemma after about 15 MRTA rebels stormed the diplomatic residence on Dec. 17 and captured more than 500 guests attending a lavish embassy reception. Should he take immediate military action or pursue a negotiated solution?
To the surprise of many, given Fujimori's traditional toughness on communist guerrillas, he chose the latter.

Since then, within that framework of non-violence, the president has played relatively hard -- cutting basic services at the site, calling the MRTA "terrorist criminals" and, most provocatively, staging police manoeuvres outside the residence.

Recognising that a negotiated solution is the only way out without bloodshed, however, the president also appointed a low-profile negotiator, established communications with the MRTA and floated a proposal for safe passage to a third country if the rebels release all the remaining hostages.

Although the police manoeuvres brought one of the most serious incidents in the crisis on Monday when rebels fired on police for the first time, Fujimori's tactics have prevented bloodshed so far and sent his approval rating up by about five percentage points to above 50 percent in opinion polls. But they have brought no tangible progress in the standoff.

"The positive thing about the government's handling of the hostage crisis is that there has been no bloodshed. However, they have not achieved a solution because the MRTA are still inside the embassy," opposition legislator Javier Alva Orlandini said.
The government and the rebels agreed in principle to talks but are deadlocked over the issue of freeing 400 imprisoned MRTA members.
Japan, which has two dozen captives in the residence, has broadly backed Fujimori from the outset, although Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto strongly criticised the police manoeuvres at the site.
The United States, which has sent security advisers to Peru, has given several resounding endorsements to Fujimori.

But, however successful Fujimori's day-to-day handling of the crisis, he will inevitably come under fire when the dust settles on the wider issue of how his security apparatus failed to prevent the MRTA takeover in the first place.
